title: The Breakdown of Classical Minicrypt Equivalences in the Quantum-Computation Classical-Communication Model
authors: Boyang Chen, Yiming Wang, Ziyi Xie
abstract: Classically, it is well-known that several fundamental cryptographic primitives, including one-way functions, pseudorandom number generators, commitments, and signatures, characterize the same cryptographic world, which is known as "Minicrypt". In this paper, we investigate to what extent this picture persists in the quantum-computation classical-communication (QCCC) setting, where parties may perform quantum local computation, but communicate through only classical messages. We demonstrate that the classical Minicrypt landscape breaks down in the QCCC model by oracle separations. We construct two oracle worlds where efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles (EV-OWPuzz) exist. By a known equivalence, QCCC one-time signatures also exist in both worlds. In the first, one-way functions do not exist, even if we allow quantum pseudodeterministic evaluation. In the second, QCCC bit commitments do not exist. Thus, the classical Minicrypt reductions from signatures to one-way functions and bit commitments have no fully black-box counterparts in the QCCC setting. Our proofs develop techniques for analyzing the random phase states, including a concentration theorem and an LOCC decoupling theorem, which may be of independent interest.
summary: This paper analyzes the limits of cryptographic security in a quantum setting where computation is quantum but communication is classical (QCCC). It proves that the classical equivalence of cryptographic tools breaks down by constructing oracle worlds where certain primitives, like one-way functions, cannot be simulated from others. The work develops advanced quantum information tools to establish these fundamental separations.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the classical equivalence of fundamental cryptographic primitives (Minicrypt) holds when computation is restricted to the Quantum-Computation Classical-Communication (QCCC) model.
main_result: The classical Minicrypt landscape breaks down in the QCCC model, demonstrated by oracle separations showing that primitives like one-way functions and bit commitments do not have fully black-box counterparts.
method: The authors construct specific oracle worlds and employ advanced quantum information techniques, including concentration theorems and the Hilbert-valued Efron–Stein inequality, to prove these separations.
model_or_system: The core model is the QCCC setting, where quantum local computation is possible, but communication is restricted to classical messages. The analysis revolves around cryptographic primitives like One-Way Puzzles (EV-OWPuzz) and commitment schemes.
key_observables: The primary observables are the existence or non-existence of specific cryptographic primitives (e.g., OWFs, bit commitments) relative to the oracle structure.
important_parameters: The analysis depends on the complexity of the oracle access (unitary oracle model) and the parameters governing the security reduction, such as the error bounds $\epsilon$ and $\delta$.
main_assumptions: The results are shown to hold in the unitary-oracle access model, and some constructions rely on the assumption that the puzzle distribution is $\epsilon$-close to uniform.
figures_summary: Figure 1 provides an intuitive visualization of known black-box reductions and oracle separations among QCCC primitives.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the general problem in the QCCC model, then developing tools like the Hilbert-valued Efron–Stein inequality, and finally applying these tools to construct separations proving the breakdown of classical cryptographic equivalences.
why_interesting: The techniques developed, such as the concentration theorems and the generalization of classical inequalities (Efron-Stein) to quantum states, are highly relevant for analyzing information flow and security in quantum communication protocols.
